newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania sees inflation falling in years to 2000.
newsitem.headline: Romania sees inflation falling in years to 2000.

text.p: Year-on-year inflation in Romania is expected to slow to 30 percent in 1998 after an estimated 97 percent this year, and to 20 percent in 1999, a government document showed on Monday.
The document outlining Romania's economic development before the turn of the century said 12-month inflation was expected to ease to 15 percent by the year 2000.

In a first stage, the economic policy will focus on macro- economic stability, working to fight inflation, strengthen financial discipline and slash the budget and current account deficits, the document said.

"The attainment of our targets by stepping up structural reforms will help the economy to adapt to the macro-economic demands imposed by long-term high-rate economic growth, all while furthering anti-inflationary policy," the document said.

The document, worked out by the Economic Reform Council of the new centrist coalition government, said macro-economic stability measures would rely on deep reforms to cut losses in farming and in large energy-consuming sectors.

Central bank governor Mugur Isarescu recently said the ambitious inflation target for 1998 could be attained only in the presence of tough reforms, including privatisation, economic restructuring and tight monetary and fiscal policies.
Romania's new government, which ousted leftists in last November's polls, has embarked on a radical reform package to revive the economy and win international support.
Romania had monthly inflation of 6.9 percent in April, down from 30.7 percent in March. Year-on-year inflation in April was 176.8 percent. Expected inflation in May is six percent.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea last month ruled out any inflationary shocks in the months ahead, after the government liberalised fuel, energy and food prices earlier this year.
One of the main objectives of Ciorbea's reform programme -- agreed with international lenders -- is to reduce monthly inflation to about two percent in the second half of 1997.

The International Monetary Fund approved credits totalling $430 million for Romania in April. Last month, the World Bank pledged $630 million in loans, showing appreciation for the Romanian government's progress in introducing reforms.
